Since then, it’s been smaller things that I’ve found, but more so the bigger deal here is that no matter if you’re using Flock or Axon or whatever it is — because now you have Axon and Motorola also launching their own private networks outside of the National Crime Information Center — the person on this network with the worst security hygiene is going to be as secure as the entire network will be. That’s the big problem.
If I were to have it my way, police officers would not have access to Flock at all. If I were to have it my way, you wouldn’t have this level of surveillance at all. But let’s just say if I were to have it my way on security policy, a police department would have one person who is trained and has a lot of security hygiene and privacy hygiene and is trained to look up Flock searches for police officers. But what we’re seeing is a lot of police chiefs who have Flock accounts. Why would a police chief ever even need to use this service? It’s their job to manage the department.
In the action movie, the cops usually have to bribe the person with access to the surveillance tool with cookies and booze to run a search without a warrant, right?
Yeah, and they usually have bifocals and are really smart.
We’ve been conditioned to think that’s how it should work. At the very least, there should be some light bribery involved, not free access. I am not a security expert by any means. I’ve been covering tech for a long time, and it just strikes me that there are some very basic concepts about security that Flock in particular missed.
The idea that we have open access, there are no access controls, that they were practicing what is called security by obscurity. You could just drive a truck through it and they would deny it. All that seems very basic. Is it just that they’re a startup and they didn’t know any better?
I think they knew better and they didn’t have to do anything about it, because nobody made them. Because somehow across America, police departments and city councils and senators and your federal government allowed these cameras to be put up everywhere without any type of security test or any type of security protocol, any type of triage for what to do if something goes wrong. None of that exists.
Circling back, when I’m actually sitting there in front of the Senate, I’m not going to say, “I can’t believe how bad Flock is.” Flock is a for-profit tech startup. Of course they’re going to do whatever they can to stay competitive. That’s their job that we give them as a society. The job of a legislator is to protect us from them. Because even when we yell at police for the privacy stuff, you wouldn’t consider a police officer or a police department to be Fourth Amendment defenders. They would be on the other side of that argument.
We need somebody on the side that actually defends people’s privacy. Our government has been utterly asleep at the wheel, especially when it comes to security vulnerabilities, but that’s across the board. That’s everywhere. Right now, it’s actually a really terrifying time that we’re in.
You recently testified in front of the Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime and Counterterrorism. That was a hearing about Flock. That subcommittee is chaired by Josh Hawley, who’s a Republican. He opened a probe into Flock.
I’m curious about that experience, preparing for that testimony and what message you wanted to send. But I just want to note that it is remarkable that a Republican is holding hearings into law enforcement technology and whether or not it’s appropriate, and that’s happening across the country.
What do you make of that? That it’s this bipartisan? Is it that everyone’s just woken up to civil liberties? This is a convenient punching bag, and everyone hates tech? How do you see the shape of it?
For any politician at the Senate level, there’s going to be theater. I don’t consider that to be a meeting where there’s going to be a solution at the end.
But what I did do there, in full transparency, is I wanted to testify with the C-SPAN cameras on in front of a Senate committee, explaining that things like FISA 702 or CORCA — these things that a lot of these politicians, even some people on that subcommittee, co-sponsored — are massive risks to privacy and security.
Because you can’t say that they didn’t know when an expert witness who’s a hacker told them in testimony. That’s ultimately why I went to Washington, DC, because I knew that it would be basically just a bunch of people proudly saying that they’re angry at Flock because everybody’s angry at Flock.
A lot of the things in Hawley’s proposals are things that Flock is already kind of doing, in their own defense, which is good news. It’s not to choose one over the other. Both are actually taking positions that are big compromises from where they probably stood a year or two years ago.
It was a wild experience. It was strange. They expected me to just talk about how bad Flock was. I really didn’t really see a purpose to that. If I wanted to scream about how bad Flock is now, I would just contact somebody at Flock and say, “We need to talk about this. I’m really mad about the security vulnerability,” because they do talk to me now. If I find a security vulnerability, I tell them about it and they take it seriously. Of course it took a lot of damage for them to take me seriously.
But if I’m standing in front of the Senate, I’m going to say, “Why don’t you do something? Because this is your job and this is what we voted for you to do.” As far as the bipartisan stuff, I’m really happy about it, honestly. It’s great. It’s awesome to see our country agree on anything as a whole right now. That’s wonderful.
A lot of Republicans remember COVID and they remember mask mandates and stuff and they probably imagine what a Flock camera would do in that situation. It might automatically send them a ticket or an arrest warrant for leaving their house during lockdown. Who knows? But that is all related to privacy risks and authoritarianism and it’s all very real in their memory.
It is interesting to see a lot of politicians take the side of ICE and take the side of the National Guard driving into a city where the police department doesn’t even want them there, and then also be anti-Flock or anti-surveillance. It’s an interesting time.
There’s something there. One of my early career rookie mistakes was that I covered telecom companies and ISPs as a baby blogger at AOL and I got it into my head that I should testify in front of Congress to talk about how the ISPs were charging everybody too much money.
I called the general counsel and the policy office at AOL and I said, “Can you get me in front of Congress?” They said, “About what?” And I said, “The ISPs are bad,” and they went, “You know, we’re an ISP,” and that was the end of that conversation. It didn’t go any farther.
[Laughs] You definitely need a lawyer if you’re going to testify in front of the Senate. There are a lot of legal expenses involved. It’s pretty stressful all in all. I feel like a lot of people think it’s a lucky thing, but  it’s a very stressful two weeks of your life.
You are in the center of that swirl, and it is bipartisan. I would put up surveillance and data centers as the issues that are uniting Americans today. Are you hearing from both sides? Did you sit with Republican senators individually? I’m sure you hear from regular people on both sides of the aisle.
Is it really that we don’t want the government to spy on us, so we’re going to yell at these cameras? Or is it bigger than that?
I think, and what I hope, is that when people discover what’s going on with Flock, and what’s going on with other police surveillance technology, they also don’t immediately go to misinformation, because that’s what a lot of people do. A lot of people will hear about the Flock cameras and then they’ll go, “How is Israel involved in this?” Then they immediately go down that rabbit hole on X or 4chan and then it builds this conspiracy theory that’s completely not in parity with the actual problem that we’re trying to solve.
What always entertains me so much about those types of conspiracies is that reality is just as crazy. It’s just as wild. There’s just as much outrage in reality. Somehow conspiracies are more attractive, even though on many occasions they’re not even as interesting as reality.
LexisNexis, for example, is a data broker that police use, that your car uses, that your devices sell data to constantly. If people knew the average amount of data that this data broker has about them that’s being sold and traded constantly, I feel like their anger about Flock would be completely eclipsed by it.
Can I connect those thoughts? I’ve been thinking about this a lot. Five years ago, we could confidently write a story debunking the notion that Instagram was listening to you. [Instagram CEO] Adam Mosseri, this poor man, has to make a video once a week insisting that he is not listening to you. Part of the reason that five years ago we would be confident in writing that story is the technological cost of listening to every Instagram user and figuring out what they had said to serve you ads was actually very high.
It was much cheaper to say, “You were on your friend’s Wi-Fi network six months ago, they searched for vacations, we’re going to serve you the ads and the coincidence will be astounding and you will believe that we’re listening to you, but it’s actually just a bunch of like data matrix synthesis, right? But that’s going to be very effective.”
We could write that story and say, “Actually you were in the same place at the same time. There’s no way they’re listening to you, it would be too expensive.” But here in 2026, I’m not sure I can make that claim anymore. Everyone wants to listen to you all the time. The amount of databases that we are synthesizing have skyrocketed all the way to “I’ve seen all the license plates on all the highways at all times, and the police chief has that data.”
How do you regain a sense of privacy? There’s a part of me that says so many people believe their phones are listening to them that you can never claw your way back, that you can never end the conspiracy theory.
The “phone listening to you” thing is so interesting to me because it’s one of those perfect examples of conspiracy versus reality, where if somebody is having a discussion about something, like that they want to get a horse. Weird example. But I was thinking about learning how to ride a horse. You have that discussion with your partner and then later on that day, you get a suggestion or an ad for horse-riding lessons on your phone. The conclusion and the conspiracy theory is my phone is listening to my conversations.
That’s pretty reasonable until you find out that it’s very inefficient for them to do so. The crazy part is that you’ve been giving subtle hints to Meta, to Google, and to all these companies and they have an algorithm that can figure out that you’re going to want horse-riding lessons and so when you feel like your phone’s been recording your conversations, it’s almost like this glitch in the matrix where you have a moment to realize how powerful the algorithm actually is at predicting what you’re about to think. That is scary and that’s not a conspiracy. That’s actually how it works.
That always boggles my mind like that. Wow, look at the real thing happening because it’s so much crazier than the conspiracy is. Of course they could listen to you. There are a lot of devices that listen to you that say they’re using your data to self-improve. Tesla listens to you. Like there’s a lot of different services and products.
But the scary part is that listening to your conversation is one of the least efficient and least valuable things it could do because it already has so much more important information. What you’re communicating verbally is usually not nearly as valuable as just your subtle pattern.
Yeah, and your transaction history. I guess what I’m getting at is again, five years ago, I would say some version of that all the time: “They’re not listening to you. The real thing is way scarier and listening to you isn’t valuable.” And it would be costly. You have to store all this audio, you have to process it, you have to figure it out. And now it feels like actually it’s not costly. It is happening all around us all the time.
If I look at Flock, the problems break down into two buckets. One, the very idea of a private database that anyone can search without controls is bad. And we should legislate a bunch of controls around that thing. And then two, letting a startup kind of YOLO that technology into the world without any security best practices, equally bad. These are two different problems that have come together to create a privacy disaster.
But even if you think Axon or Motorola will have better security, you’ve got the first problem, which is you need controls around these private networks. All that in my mind is right next to the conspiracy style thinking you’re describing, where it’s technologically plausible that all the bad things are happening.
I can’t rule them out anymore. My Apple Watch might just make transcripts of all the meetings without anyone’s permission. The loophole you describe in our legal system for years, the idea that you don’t have privacy in public, has been a lodestar. It is just foundational, and now people don’t love that anymore. Because the idea that you don’t have privacy in public enables a bunch of people to do a bunch of things people don’t like.
Maybe we should rethink that as a moral, ethical, and legal matter, but we’re nowhere close to that. I just feel like all that is pouring fuel on the conspiracy theories. You’re in the center of the storm here, and so I’m wondering if you can find a rational set of policy outcomes here that tamps down on those flames.
A little over a year ago, when my first video on Flock came out, if the company’s response and the government’s response to it was, “Audit logs are now going to be open and they’re going to exist on something that uses immutable data storage. It could be the blockchain, could be WORM or something like that. Basically, anybody can look at them, anybody can own them, nobody can change them…”
If they said that, then they immediately went and fixed all the security vulnerabilities and you just had a smarter way of looking at these things… Also one thing that would have been really interesting around them is to be able to go to your DMV and show them your license and opt out.
You could say, “I’ve not been convicted of a felony, I’ve not done anything wrong, I don’t want to be tracked.” And then all of a sudden, when a Flock license plate reader detects your plate, it says “opt out,” unless a cop puts you on a hot list because you’ve murdered someone or something like that. These are all reasonable compromises that could have been made with relatively little expense.
But now a year later, who’s going to trust anybody who makes those compromises? Now there’s no trust anymore because of that. Because Flock dug its heels in so much, and because police departments constantly gaslit everybody over and over again with, “There’s no abuse, there’s no record of abuse. We’re checking it. We’re checking these audit logs constantly. It makes you safer. If you take these cameras down, your kids are going to go missing.” That type of thing.
Now how can you fix this? Now people are just destroying cameras. Now, people are just threatening executives of these companies because that’s what they do when they get taken this far out.
That’s my big problem now. If I have any goal in this or any dog in this fight, I’d like to bring people back towards solutionism, because I don’t want surveillance at all, but we don’t live in Benn Jordistan. We live in a democracy and a lot of people are okay with it to some degree. Most people are not okay with it, from polling I’ve done, if it doesn’t involve a warrant.
Somewhere along there is a solution where nobody’s happy, but everybody’s content. If I could do anything right now, it would be bringing people back towards a path where a solution can be found.
One of the things I’ve been thinking about a lot is the widespread assumption that surveillance does exist. When there’s some high profile crime, the assumption that there will be cameras that will show us something about this crime actually kind of redounds in favor of the surveillance companies. Ring had an ad at the Super Bowl about tracking lost dogs. They got in a lot of trouble over what else we’re going to do with this surveillance network.
I think it was a week later that Savannah Guthrie’s mom was kidnapped and Jamie was on every news network in town saying Ring cameras are going to solve it, whether or not the footage that we saw was even from Ring cameras.
There was this notion that surveillance would help. That is a real pendulum swing back and forth. The cameras are the solution at one time and the abstract concept of the cameras makes people mad because why are you passively surveilling me? You’re talking about solutions. How do you thread that needle?
Most people need to understand, especially police departments, that most of the things that are being promised by people like Garrett Langley, the CEO of Flock, and Jamie Siminoff, the CEO of Ring, are their sales tactics. These CEOs or executives or anybody from any company, they’re not actually going out and doing this research in a way where they’re not cherry-picking data and looking for statistics that support their product.
You could say that’s unethical, you could say that’s wrong, but that’s what you expect from a tech company. Nobody believes that a tech company would all of a sudden become a humanitarian while they’re still representing their company. We could take that and we could isolate that, and then we say, “Research needs to be done,” and research is very, very complicated for this.
In sociology and criminology, we don’t even understand if increasing police reduces crime as a society. We’ve not even proven that. Putting cameras up is a really big ask. We just need to be asking these questions a lot more, and being more careful about putting these cameras up. What will they actually help?
If we could find something that actually helps, we could say, “We have a lot of cars being stolen in this neighborhood. Hey guys, how do you feel about an ALPR that has 24 hours of retention time coming up in this neighborhood and everything that we search on it will be in an immutable audit log that you’ll be able to see every single day? How do you feel about that?” I feel like a lot more people would say, “Yeah, I don’t want my car stolen.” They would maybe err on the side of trying something to reduce a crime problem rather than the police just behind closed doors signing a multi-million dollar contract to put cameras up all over the city without asking anyone.
That’s one of the first solutions. Transparency in general. If I were running Flock in some weird parallel universe, a year ago when Have I Been Flocked? came out — the website that allows you to search your own license plate — I would have immediately partnered with them. I would have said, “Here’s all our data. Thank you for running this. Let’s give you some money so you can keep this server running fast. Because I want everybody to not be mad at us. I want everybody to understand what’s going on.”
A lot of it comes down to quantifying things at a local level to see what people want, and maybe even having referendums in certain places. Referendums are usually really tricky and you have your Brexit situations with referendums, but sometimes they’re also useful.
For a general person watching this right now, the one thing that I strongly urge is to find out who’s voting for this stuff. Find out who actually signed the paperwork to spend the money on it without any form of security vulnerability check, without any sort of special license or any sort of audit data, without going through anything else, because that person is typically a city council member and you can run and be one of those quite easily.
It’s not that difficult. Most city council members that I’ve met are just like me, just like my viewers. They’re not these prestigious politicians. It’s something that most people could do if they have a few friends helping them campaign.
You said immutable record again and it reminded me that earlier you earned the distinction of being the only person on Decoder to ever suggest the blockchain as a solution for something in a way that did not immediately imply that you would make a bunch of money. I want to congratulate you for that.
[Laughs] It’s interesting that all of this ALPR stuff blew up at the same time that crypto and blockchain and NFTs blew up. Yet nobody ever thought, “Hey, we could use a proof-of-stake network, one that’s not actually scorching the Earth to solve Sudoku puzzles, but we can actually use a highly efficient proof-of-stake network to immutably store data for these audit logs.”
But it’s not too late. These things still exist. You don’t have to use blockchain. There’s IPFS, which is a decentralized file system. There’s WORM, which is “write once, read many.” That’s a thing that IBM, I think, invented, but it’s used everywhere. There are a lot of ways to do immutable data, but it being democratized data is what’s the most important part.
[Laughs] We’re not using the GPUs for Sudoku puzzles anymore. We’re running them red hot for other stuff. Don’t worry. We switched those over.
You mentioned working with the companies. You mentioned the idea that Flock is now partnering with some of its critics, which would have helped them early. They have invited you in, right? One of your strongest calls is for external auditors and researchers to evaluate these systems. It’s one of the things you said was needed in your congressional hearing.
They’ve invited you in. You’re now a third-party reviewer with Flock. What is your relationship with Flock like now? And do you think it’s changed how you view and evaluate the company?
There are certainly people at the company who really dislike me. And then there are people at the company… I’ve spoken to the CEO. I’ve spoken to a couple of the executives. There are people at the company who are absolutely willing to have a conversation and figure out what a solution actually looks like. Unfortunately, and I say “unfortunately” because throwing poop is really easy, but cleaning up the room so people can sit in it again without smelling poop is really hard, and most people are only willing to do the throwing poop part.
But one thing that happens in our society all too often is when we have a big controversy, especially on social media, and then there is no remediation at all. There’s no allowance for remediation. If you think about somebody getting canceled or something, one thing I always think is, “What do you want them to do? What should they do now? Do you have any ideas or should they just die?” Because that’s not a solution.
We can’t just snap our fingers. If, in the next month, Flock just said, “We can’t do it anymore. We’re going out of business. We quit. We’re going to make toys or something else, or we’re going to just leave,” Axon, Verkada, Palantir, and all these other companies would just step in and do the exact same thing and they would learn from Flock’s mistakes and do it more efficiently.
We’re in a place right now where, had Flock not dug their heels in and not listened to press strategies that make them seem more confident than they actually are, and actually had listened to people and maybe worked on a solution — it’s going to be rough and I’m going to get a lot of hate for even suggesting that that’s a thing — but if we actually want to solve this problem, we have to do that.
You have to have an olive branch. You could still hit back. You can still wear a boxing glove in one hand, but you have to have an olive branch in the other one. Otherwise, I can’t fix this myself as a YouTuber. One of the more powerful things — and this is almost two months ago — was someone high up at Flock said, “We want guardrails. Give us some guardrails. Just tell us what to do. Tell us what to do, and we’ll make the changes we need to do and stay in business and grow that way. But we need those guardrails.”
Unfortunately, the people who make those guardrails are just saying, “I don’t like Flock. Flock is bad.” They’re not actually setting these guardrails up. You also have a lot of different bills being passed around election time. I just wish a lot of these people would get together in one room with Flock and make a decision on what they think would be best to move forward.
You’ve made some very aggressive YouTube videos about Flock. One of my favorites was you went to the Flock Forward convention where they banned you. They canceled your hotel room, and then you set up Wi-Fi scanners and Bluetooth scanners outside. You figured out who was there.
This is perfect stunt journalism. I watched that video and I went, “I should stop running this fussy web magazine and I should just do this.” It was a great video with a super aggressive posture towards Flock.
Can you still be in that mode when you’re in the company trying to help create solutions?
It’s a great question that I think about all the time. It’s really difficult to be a journalist in that type of situation where you’re talking to the company and you’re producing things that harm the company or its public image at the same time.
At the end of the day, you just can’t lie. You just have to be as honest as possible, which is one of the reasons I’m even saying that I’ve spoken to the Flock CEO and stuff like that. Because I just want to have a 360-degree understanding and find out as much information as I possibly can, and then let my viewers decide how they feel about that.
Maybe the only thing I really want to guide them toward at this point is away from things like violence, away from things like threatening the CEO, because that actually makes us less safe as a society. That also makes cops more likely to put cameras up everywhere. It’s not a very good way of dealing with the issue and also just threatening or terrorizing people’s families is not a solution for anything.
That’s a question I think about constantly because it’s really, really hard to navigate this ethically, knowing that your next story might hurt the person you just had a conversation with, or vice versa, that the person you just had a conversation with might actually make your audience think less of you or judge you in some way.
But I truly do believe that if you hang onto nuance as much as possible, and if you’re always sort of letting nuance guide you, that in the long term it’ll be very bumpy, but in the long term you’ll be rewarded for it. That’s maybe why my channel gets the views it does. I hope, or I like to think that, and maybe it’s egotistical to think that, but I think it’s because I always try to hang on to nuance to some extent.
I always say, “To be fair,” and then look at that side because otherwise I’m just making content that’s telling people how to think. Whereas I feel like people want to be led on a mission to discover things and learn about things and then come up with their own opinion afterwards.
I’m glad you brought this up because I wanted to end with a little bit of you as a YouTuber, as a person who tries to gain an audience on these platforms. One of my longstanding jokes on the show is every YouTuber gets their wings when they make a video about how mad they are at YouTube, about the algorithm or demonetization or whatever YouTube thing.
Marques Brownlee just made a video about how mad he is at YouTube about A/B testing. It took a long time, but here we are. You’re describing succeeding on an algorithmic platform with nuance, with data, and with journalism. I look at the algorithmic platforms and I think that doesn’t exist.
What’s your relationship like there? If you’re a self-described YouTuber, are you on the road to becoming MrBeast? Can you still fight the fight?
I don’t try to analyze it. If I get a video that doesn’t have a million views or something, I don’t say that video is a failure. I think that video really worked probably for the demographic that watched it and then it didn’t work for another slice of the demographic. In terms of nuance, enough people are exhausted from being told how to think about it and they feel like they’re being worked nonstop when they’re on social media and watching things.
Maybe that nuance helps my channel provide some form of relief from that. I try to do better and better. And it’s interesting because maybe my content will be less exciting if I try to be more and more nuanced. But I speak to a lot of journalists. Brendan Keefe from Atlanta News First is a great example. I would almost consider him a mentor at this point because he’s extremely rigid with his nuance and with his ethics.
A good example is that Flock Forward thing that you mentioned. Before that, I had found the entire guest list. I had opened up and downloaded the app and then decompiled the app and probed it and found the entire guest list and a bunch of information about all of the guests who were going to Flock Forward. This is valuable info. These are police officers and senators, and most of these guests, our tax dollars paid for them to fly to Atlanta to come to this event.
Immediately I told a couple of journalists and they said, “Yes, give it to me,” and I thought to myself, like, “No, this is wrong. I need to report this to the company if I want to actually have principles. If I want to stay on this side of things, if I want to be able to tell police that they can’t search their wives because it’s personal information that they’re not supposed to see, then I also can’t release breach data.” It’s those types of things that are really hard. That would have been a banger video for me to release that guest list. But over the long run, that actually pays off.
People just watch your content and feel like you’re more trustworthy, which is the number one area where people struggle with YouTube or any sort of social media, because you have to somehow say, “I actually have standards and ethics and I’m going to try and tell you the truth in this crazy noise.” That’s what I’m trying to do. I don’t know if I’m going to achieve it, but that’s a big goal of mine.
I can’t agree with that more. Anybody who listens to our other show The Vergecast knows that I prattle on about our ethics policy all the time. In this media environment, you actually have to make the subtext text and say, “I made this information this way. This process generated this outcome.” It’s the process that you actually are buying from me, not the headline.
There’s something about that that I think is very challenging on a platform like YouTube. That’s why I asked about it. Because you can see what the platform naturally wants to do and you’ve managed to grow a lot with very in-depth coverage about very wonky topics that our elected officials would maybe prefer not to know about and that’s a success.
I’m just wondering if you fight the platform’s dynamics openly and explicitly, if you think about them, or if you’re just riding the wave.
My ultimate wish — which you know, unfortunately isn’t going to come true — is that I can make a video about Unitree robots, let’s say, and then find a security vulnerability, find a backdoor, which I did, and then some of my viewers actually take that research and improve on it and make it better. And then continue doing that, and then that actually results in something bigger and then I’m able to just move on to something else entirely.
It doesn’t work that way. I’m still talking about Flock, and I’m still talking about data centers. I’m still talking about storing an image in a bird. All these things I’m still constantly connected to.
But looking past just the views and retention and looking towards the reason I made that Flock Forward video was because a lot of my viewers saw that and said, “Whoa, whoa, whoa, what is that? A [software-defined radio]? You can listen to that stuff. How do you do that?” And now they’re into radio, which is crazy. There are so many more interesting things than listening to a bunch of Flock employees talking on a wireless microphone with radio.
It encourages people to sort of explore with tools that they could pretty easily obtain. I hope that that results in more people doing more interesting things in collecting and processing data in ways that actually help the world.
I can’t think of a better place to leave it than there. Benn, thank you so much for being on Decoder. Like I said, this was a dream come true.
Thank you for having me. I appreciate it.
items.content: Today, I’m talking with Benn Jordan, musician, YouTuber, researcher, and investigative journalist. You might know Benn from those first two titles — he’s got a prolific discography of experimental music dating back decades.But in the last couple of years, he’s become a high-profile face in the creator and media spaces for his work investigating Flock Safety, the maker of automatic license plate readers and the software that powers them.Benn recently testified in front of Congress, at a hearing the Senate Judiciary Committee’s Subcommittee on Crime and Counterterrorism held, dedicated to Flock and other ALPR systems. This hearing felt like the culmination of months and months of growing criticism and bipartisan backlash against Flock — all of which is taking a shape similar to the pushback against AI data centers.Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.This has led to major fallout for Flock. Hundreds of cities, counties, and other local governments have begun canceling contracts, and Flock is now under investigation by Republican Sen. Josh Hawley. Last week, Reuters reported that Flock plans to cut about 18 percent of its workforce.So of course I wanted to dig into all of that with Benn, not just because he played a role in that, but because he’s also become in some ways the face of a new front in the broader debate about surveillance and privacy.A point you’ll hear Benn make is that he doesn’t actually hate Flock as a company — he thinks its posture toward critics has been a colossal PR failure that made it low-hanging fruit, while competitors like Axon and Motorola quietly build the same kind of networks. Instead, Benn now talks to Flock directly, including to its CEO Garrett Langley, and reports security vulnerabilities to the company when he finds them. (As a side note: we have also invited Flock’s CEO on the show; Garrett if you’re listening, we would love to have you.)Benn says his outreach to the company is an olive branch he’s extended to Flock as part of his goal of working toward real, tangible solutions to surveillance overreach, rather than part of a crusade to tear one single company down.That’s a real theme throughout our conversation: that Flock and other high profile names in surveillance are just part of the problem — our real focus should be on the interlocking relationship between private industry, government, and law enforcement that prioritizes secrecy over transparency.We never voted for an insecure network of cameras on every street corner, and we’re certainly not being asked if we’re comfortable with access to this network being given to police officers with a penchant for abusing it. So Benn sees his work on YouTube and with other researchers, civil rights groups, and journalists as an accountability function that forces this conversation to the forefront. And so far, it’s working.Okay: Benn Jordan on Flock, privacy, and the new surveillance backlash. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.Benn Jordan, you’re a musician, YouTuber, and researcher. Lately you’ve been an investigative journalist. You are a witness in Senate hearings. Welcome to Decoder.Thanks for having me.I’m a huge fan of yours. It’s just a delight to have you here. A lot of people in the Verge audience know you as a musician, but lately you have been relentlessly focused on Flock cameras, which are automatic license-plate readers (ALPRs). You recently testified in front of a Senate hearing on those cameras and the surveillance they enable.Give us a sense of your background. For people who don’t know you or haven’t been following you for years, where did Benn Jordan come from and how did you end up being the person who makes videos about Flock?I’ve been a musician my entire life, pretty much. I’ve also always been kind of a hacker, or somebody who is that type of person who always takes stuff apart. If I get a product that wants me to pay for a service that’s already in the product, then that’s a puzzle I want to solve and I get excited about it. But a lot of times that blends into investigative journalism as well.With the Flock stuff, it’s just that I live in Atlanta, which has more Flock cameras than anywhere else per square mile. About two years ago I started noticing them. I thought they were traffic cameras or something like that. Then I started looking into what they were actually doing and then started looking into things like security vulnerabilities. More than anything, everything that’s happening right now in the public, in the news, has to do with people just figuring out that these have existed the entire time.A lot of my focus now is on the lack of transparency from the government, because the companies are always going to make money and try to make as much money as they can, especially if it’s from taxpayer money. But in this case, I feel like our government missed it. And that’s where we’re at.There’s a question that’s been rattling around my head the entire time we’ve been having what I would call the modern privacy and surveillance debate.When I say “modern,” what I mean is it feels like we woke up sometime in the last year and everything is recording us all the time and everything is watching us and the glasses have cameras in them and Mark Zuckerberg is saying phones don’t have a light, and that is meant to end a conversation.That’s it. That’s the argument. Phones don’t have a light, no further questions. The Apple Watch is going to start doing automatic transcriptions, and everyone said, “Wait, hold on. No thank you. We actually don’t want this to happen.” But my personal experience of this is that my political coming of age was the Iraq War and the Patriot Act.This is the stuff that people were talking about twenty-five years ago — don’t do warrantless wiretaps, don’t make the databases all connect to each other so you can take the metadata and de-anonymize people at will.What is it about this time that has made everybody so angry? Because we could have been angry twenty-five years ago.I’m always trying to get people more informed on the information that’s being collected about them every time they go to a website, every time they sign up for something, every time they check into a restaurant online, every time they use their phone. In this case, one of the reasons that people are really upset about is that you can’t opt out. That’s the first thing.I can’t say, “I don’t want these Flock cameras or Axon cameras or whatever they are tracking my every move and giving it to law enforcement.” I have no option to do that. I was never given an option on whether to vote for them or vote for somebody who was in favor of them. It just kind of happened and you know people weren’t told about them. That would be the first thing — that you can still install a separate OS on an Android phone or you could turn off Wi-Fi and Bluetooth or just leave your phone at home. Whereas now you can’t actually go to the grocery store without somebody tracking your vehicle.The second thing is that — and this is kind of related to opting in and opting out — I can pay for a new AI smartwatch or I can pay for an Amazon Echo device or something like that, or I cannot. Whereas this way I’m paying for this already. This is just my property taxes going up and I’m paying for surveillance.In some ways it is the same as the NSA, but I feel like it’s much more local now.You don’t get to go to the town board meeting and yell at the NSA. Although maybe you should. Honestly, that might be good for everyone. There is that part of it, and you’ve certainly been at a bunch of local town board meetings. I’ve watched a lot of videos of you talking to them and helping other people articulate their concerns.That, to me, is one of the more fascinating aspects of all this. Flock went from a company that was selling cameras to everyone, and the idea that adding Flock cameras would increase the safety of your town went from all but assumed to, “Hold on, we all have a lot of questions,” and now this company is struggling a little bit. They’re losing contracts, they are retrenching, their communication strategy has changed.What do you make of that? Is that just the power of local democracy in action, or is there something else?It definitely is democracy in action. That’s the good news. The best news out of anything that’s happened is that with both Flock and data centers, it’s two things that have made people actually look up who their mayor is and who their city council members are and show up to meetings and then get involved in those local politics.Because those local politics affect your life way more than national politics. They just don’t make the headlines. We’re not as involved. Your day-to-day following what Donald Trump is doing is likely not going to make that big of a difference other than what you argue about over Thanksgiving. Whereas local politics, that’s straight up, in the next year, going to have a big effect on your life.People are getting involved in that, and then in cases like Asheville, North Carolina, where it’s actually changing the political landscape. People are so dissatisfied with the surveillance policies of their local politicians that it looks like that they may have a new mayor as a result of it, who also comes with a bunch of other interesting and progressive ideas that would probably help the city a lot more than the current mayor has.That’s a big deal right there. The other part that discourages me a little bit, or the part that I find a little disappointing, is that Flock has become this buzzword, but a lot of people don’t look beyond that. I just heard in the race for governor in Georgia that the Democratic candidate yesterday talked about getting rid of Flock cameras and being anti-Flock, when this is somebody who as mayor of Atlanta welcomed Flock. You see a lot of that happening now, too, where they just say “Flock bad” and then they go sign an Axon contract or they put Verkada or Motorola cameras everywhere.In my research, Flock has been the low-hanging fruit, just because they were the loudest and most defensive, whereas every other company was just taking a step back and cashing the checks.One of the pieces of the puzzle here that is just fascinating is that Flock is a startup, essentially. They’re a new company, they have a new go-to-market strategy. They talk a big game about what AI can and can’t do and with what they as a platform should and should not enable. Your Axons and your Motorolas are government contractors. They are not companies that are meant to have a personality.There’s something about Flock where Garrett Langley, the CEO, had a personality. He would go on TV and deride any critics as left-wing terrorists and that did not work. There’s something about surveillance in that case where that strategy didn’t work. There’s something about data centers where that strategy didn’t work.We just ran a big piece about the people of Utah pushing back on Kevin O’Leary, who called them all Chinese agents, and they were like, “What are you talking about?” That cut across party lines. Again, you’ve been out there. I know you’ve talked to a lot of people pushing back on surveillance.Is it just that Flock had a personality, and that enabled bipartisan pushback? Or is it surveillance more generally?In terms of the media getting attention, Flock had a lot of personality and they were very defensive. I’ve met a lot of the people from Flock who are so villainized and they don’t seem at all the way that they’ve seemed in the clips that I’ve covered in my content. It’s very different. You would assume that there’s a publicist behind a lot of this.Especially in something that serves law enforcement, where you would maybe have a publicist that’s used to dealing with Republicans and right-wing things, they just tell you to keep repeating the same thing over and over again and take a firm stance and dig your heels in. Most people who aren’t Donald Trump, when they do that, get wrecked. Flock got wrecked. They kept saying things and they kept denying security vulnerabilities and they used clever ways of reframing or redefining words and people picked up on it and now they are the villain.Whereas companies like Axon are not as sexy for a journalist. They just aren’t, and that’s probably intentional on their part. Any company that’s taking your tax dollars or trying to court your government to give your tax dollars to them probably wants to be out of the spotlight.We’ve covered Axon before. They do not want to be a company with characters. They are as anonymous as they can be.One of the things that I want to see with you on the show, most importantly of all, is to describe what a Flock camera is and what the technology behind the hardware does that makes it new.Because from watching all the videos that you make, I think, “It’s just an Android phone. They’re just putting a bunch of Android phones around town,” but it’s actually the database and the AI that makes it more dangerous than usual. Describe what the actual Flock hardware is and then how that connects to the system that makes it as controversial as it is.So ALPRs have existed, I believe, since the 1970s. They started getting used in the United States in the late 80s and 90s. One of the classic ways that they would be used in the 2000s is they would be mounted on a police car. If a police car wanted to run someone’s plate, that way they didn’t have to type it in while they’re driving, and they could run a plate over to dispatch. I personally don’t have any problem with that. I think that makes sense. That’s a decent use. However, you would have issues where you would get plate misreads and then people would get taken out of their car at gunpoint as a result.Flock is a lot different. Flock basically started a private nationwide network where any police department or city that’s using Flock’s network can opt into it and share their data with it. Police departments across the country can then run a license plate with 30 days of retention on everywhere someone’s been, anywhere in the country, as long as they’re sharing the data. You also have a lot of different bills being passed around election time. I just wish a lot of these people would get together in one room with Flock and make a decision on what they think would be best to move forward.You’ve made some very aggressive YouTube videos about Flock. One of my favorites was you went to the Flock Forward convention where they banned you. They canceled your hotel room, and then you set up Wi-Fi scanners and Bluetooth scanners outside. You figured out who was there.This is perfect stunt journalism. I watched that video and I went, “I should stop running this fussy web magazine and I should just do this.” It was a great video with a super aggressive posture towards Flock.Can you still be in that mode when you’re in the company trying to help create solutions?It’s a great question that I think about all the time. It’s really difficult to be a journalist in that type of situation where you’re talking to the company and you’re producing things that harm the company or its public image at the same time.At the end of the day, you just can’t lie. You just have to be as honest as possible, which is one of the reasons I’m even saying that I’ve spoken to the Flock CEO and stuff like that. Because I just want to have a 360-degree understanding and find out as much information as I possibly can, and then let my viewers decide how they feel about that.Maybe the only thing I really want to guide them toward at this point is away from things like violence, away from things like threatening the CEO, because that actually makes us less safe as a society. That also makes cops more likely to put cameras up everywhere. It’s not a very good way of dealing with the issue and also just threatening or terrorizing people’s families is not a solution for anything.That’s a question I think about constantly because it’s really, really hard to navigate this ethically, knowing that your next story might hurt the person you just had a conversation with, or vice versa, that the person you just had a conversation with might actually make your audience think less of you or judge you in some way.But I truly do believe that if you hang onto nuance as much as possible, and if you’re always sort of letting nuance guide you, that in the long term it’ll be very bumpy, but in the long term you’ll be rewarded for it. That’s maybe why my channel gets the views it does. I hope, or I like to think that, and maybe it’s egotistical to think that, but I think it’s because I always try to hang on to nuance to some extent.I always say, “To be fair,” and then look at that side because otherwise I’m just making content that’s telling people how to think. Whereas I feel like people want to be led on a mission to discover things and learn about things and then come up with their own opinion afterwards.I’m glad you brought this up because I wanted to end with a little bit of you as a YouTuber, as a person who tries to gain an audience on these platforms. One of my longstanding jokes on the show is every YouTuber gets their wings when they make a video about how mad they are at YouTube, about the algorithm or demonetization or whatever YouTube thing.Marques Brownlee just made a video about how mad he is at YouTube about A/B testing. It took a long time, but here we are. You’re describing succeeding on an algorithmic platform with nuance, with data, and with journalism. I look at the algorithmic platforms and I think that doesn’t exist.What’s your relationship like there? If you’re a self-described YouTuber, are you on the road to becoming MrBeast? Can you still fight the fight?I don’t try to analyze it. If I get a video that doesn’t have a million views or something, I don’t say that video is a failure. I think that video really worked probably for the demographic that watched it and then it didn’t work for another slice of the demographic. In terms of nuance, enough people are exhausted from being told how to think about it and they feel like they’re being worked nonstop when they’re on social media and watching things.Maybe that nuance helps my channel provide some form of relief from that. I try to do better and better. And it’s interesting because maybe my content will be less exciting if I try to be more and more nuanced. But I speak to a lot of journalists. Brendan Keefe from Atlanta News First is a great example. I would almost consider him a mentor at this point because he’s extremely rigid with his nuance and with his ethics.A good example is that Flock Forward thing that you mentioned. Before that, I had found the entire guest list. I had opened up and downloaded the app and then decompiled the app and probed it and found the entire guest list and a bunch of information about all of the guests who were going to Flock Forward. This is valuable info. These are police officers and senators, and most of these guests, our tax dollars paid for them to fly to Atlanta to come to this event.Immediately I told a couple of journalists and they said, “Yes, give it to me,” and I thought to myself, like, “No, this is wrong. I need to report this to the company if I want to actually have principles. If I want to stay on this side of things, if I want to be able to tell police that they can’t search their wives because it’s personal information that they’re not supposed to see, then I also can’t release breach data.” It’s those types of things that are really hard. That would have been a banger video for me to release that guest list. But over the long run, that actually pays off.People just watch your content and feel like you’re more trustworthy, which is the number one area where people struggle with YouTube or any sort of social media, because you have to somehow say, “I actually have standards and ethics and I’m going to try and tell you the truth in this crazy noise.” That’s what I’m trying to do. I don’t know if I’m going to achieve it, but that’s a big goal of mine.I can’t agree with that more. Anybody who listens to our other show The Vergecast knows that I prattle on about our ethics policy all the time. In this media environment, you actually have to make the subtext text and say, “I made this information this way. This process generated this outcome.” It’s the process that you actually are buying from me, not the headline.There’s something about that that I think is very challenging on a platform like YouTube. That’s why I asked about it. Because you can see what the platform naturally wants to do and you’ve managed to grow a lot with very in-depth coverage about very wonky topics that our elected officials would maybe prefer not to know about and that’s a success.I’m just wondering if you fight the platform’s dynamics openly and explicitly, if you think about them, or if you’re just riding the wave.My ultimate wish — which you know, unfortunately isn’t going to come true — is that I can make a video about Unitree robots, let’s say, and then find a security vulnerability, find a backdoor, which I did, and then some of my viewers actually take that research and improve on it and make it better. And then continue doing that, and then that actually results in something bigger and then I’m able to just move on to something else entirely.It doesn’t work that way. I’m still talking about Flock, and I’m still talking about data centers. I’m still talking about storing an image in a bird. All these things I’m still constantly connected to.But looking past just the views and retention and looking towards the reason I made that Flock Forward video was because a lot of my viewers saw that and said, “Whoa, whoa, whoa, what is that? A [software-defined radio]? You can listen to that stuff. How do you do that?” And now they’re into radio, which is crazy. There are so many more interesting things than listening to a bunch of Flock employees talking on a wireless microphone with radio.It encourages people to sort of explore with tools that they could pretty easily obtain. I hope that that results in more people doing more interesting things in collecting and processing data in ways that actually help the world.I can’t think of a better place to leave it than there. Benn, thank you so much for being on Decoder. Like I said, this was a dream come true.Thank you for having me. I appreciate it.
items.author: Nilay Patel
items.titleZh: 本·乔丹谈 Flock、隐私与新的监控反弹
items.descriptionZh:
这篇《Decoder》访谈围绕 Benn Jordan 与 Flock Safety 展开。Flock 是自动车牌识别系统（ALPR）及其软件平台的主要厂商，近年来在美国迅速铺开。Benn Jordan 原本是音乐人、YouTuber 和研究者，近两年因调查 Flock 而成为创作者和媒体空间中高调的调查记者。他最近在参议院司法委员会“犯罪与反恐小组委员会”的听证会上作证，该听证会专门讨论 Flock 及其他 ALPR 系统。这场听证会被视为数月来针对 Flock 的批评与两党反弹的阶段性顶点，其势头类似于此前对 AI 数据中心的抵制。随之而来的是重大商业后果：数百个城市、县和其他地方政府开始取消合同，共和党参议员 Josh Hawley 对 Flock 展开调查，路透社报道 Flock 计划裁减约 18% 的员工。

Benn 的立场并非简单“打倒 Flock”。他住在亚特兰大，那里每平方英里的 Flock 摄像头数量全美最多；大约两年前他开始注意到这些设备，随后研究其实际功能和安全漏洞。他认为 Flock 最大的问题之一是对批评者的姿态：公司及其 CEO Garrett Langley 曾把批评者称作“左翼恐怖分子”，这种强硬且防御性的公关策略让 Flock 成为最容易攻击的目标。但与此同时，Axon、Motorola、Verkada、Palantir 等竞争者正在悄悄建设同类网络。Benn 现在会直接与 Flock 沟通，包括与 CEO 交谈，并在发现安全漏洞时向公司报告。他强调，真正的问题不是某一家公司，而是私营产业、政府和执法部门之间以保密优先于透明的相互锁定关系；公众从未投票决定要在每个街角部署一个不安全的摄像头网络，也未被询问是否接受警察滥用这一网络的访问权。因此，他把自己的 YouTube 调查、与其他研究者、民权组织和记者的合作，视为一种问责机制，迫使这一对话进入公共议程。

在技术原理上，ALPR 并非新事物，自 1970 年代以来就存在，美国在 1980 年代末至 90 年代开始使用。传统方式多是把 ALPR 装在警车上，帮助警察快速查车牌，Benn 认为这类用途有一定合理性。但 Flock 的关键创新不在硬件，而在网络和数据库：它建立了私营的全国性车牌数据共享网络，任何使用 Flock 的警察局或城市都可以选择加入并共享数据。只要在共享网络中，全国各地的警察部门就能以 30 天保留期查询某人车辆在全美范围内的行踪，例如得克萨斯州的警方可以搜索某人在纽约或亚特兰大的移动轨迹，而且无需搜查令。此前，ALPR 数据共享通常必须通过国家犯罪信息中心（NCIC），需要治安法官审查整体情境并签发令状才能追踪。Flock 的法律“创新”在于把数据库私有化，从而绕开令状程序。摄像头本身并不特别先进，本质上类似 Android 设备；真正危险的是后端数据库、共享网络以及基于 AI 的查询和匹配能力。Benn 指出，虽然车辆在公共道路行驶，单点拍摄或许可类比公共场合拍照，但连续 30 天聚合一个人的行踪，所需资源若由人工完成，通常只会在极严重案件中才被批准；现在却可能被用于商店盗窃等非暴力、轻微案件。

关于“摄像头能清零犯罪”的宣传，Benn 明确反对。他认为没有证据表明 Ring 摄像头或 ALPR 能显著降低犯罪或提高破案率。更可能出现的是“犯罪转移”：有摄像头的街道犯罪减少，但隔壁没有摄像头的街区犯罪增加；如果摄像头无处不在，犯罪才无处转移。这种逻辑的终点就是全面监控。他还批评这类技术主要针对偷车、商店盗窃等行为，而非挪用公款、腐败等更严重犯罪；许多轻微犯罪背后是贫困或毒瘾问题，更应由公共政策解决，而不是把更多非暴力者送入司法系统。

安全漏洞是访谈的核心之一。Benn 发现，Flock 在 2025 年初还不要求多因素认证（MFA），并亲眼看到警察从非警察局 Wi-Fi 登录 Flock。他在暗网上找到来自俄罗斯卖家的 Flock 凭证。随后他与网络安全研究员 Jon Gaines 合作，发现摄像头存在硬件漏洞：可被诱导开启 Wi-Fi 接入点，进而完全控制 Android 设备并 root，且因发生在 Flock 生态之外而难以检测。他还发现一些 Flock 摄像头的管理界面直接暴露在互联网上，输入 IP 就能删除录像、查看 30 天前录像、上传文件或查看日志，并发现大量明文凭证。Flock 起初否认，称他只是 YouTuber、在变魔术，不是严肃安全研究者，并声称从未被黑；但 Benn 在自己机器上复现后，争议变得无可辩驳，媒体才开始关注。更大的问题是：在共享网络中，安全卫生最差的参与者会决定整个网络的安全水平。如今 Axon 和 Motorola 也在 NCIC 之外推出自己的私营网络。Benn 认为，即使 Flock 消失，Axon、Verkada、Palantir 也会接手，并从 Flock 的错误中学习，做得更高效。因此需要外部审计者和研究者，而 Flock 现在已邀请他作为第三方审查者之一，双方关系复杂但存在对话。

在国会听证会上，Benn 没有单纯抨击 Flock，而是利用 C-SPAN 镜头指出 FISA 702、CORCA 等法案对隐私和安全的巨大风险，并提醒那些曾共同提案的议员：当专家证人已在证词中说明风险时，他们不能再说“不知道”。Hawley 的调查和听证带有政治表演成分，但 Benn 认为两党对监控技术的反弹是积极信号。共和党人尤其会联想到疫情期间的口罩令和封锁，担心 Flock 摄像头被用于自动开罚单或执行居家令。与此同时，地方民主正在发挥作用：许多民众开始查市长和市议员是谁，出席地方会议， Asheville 等地的政治格局甚至可能因监控政策而改变，出现新市长候选人。但 Benn 也担心“Flock”变成口号，人们只喊“Flock 坏”，然后转向 Axon、Motorola 或 Verkada 的合同。

他提出的解决方向包括：不可篡改的审计日志，可用区块链、WORM（一次写入多次读取）或 IPFS 等实现，让公众可查看且无人能改；在车管所提供退出机制，未犯重罪者可以选择不被追踪，除非被列入重案热名单；提高透明度，在地方层面量化需求并举行公投；以及为行业设置真正的护栏。Benn 透露，Flock 高层曾表示“我们想要护栏，告诉我们该怎么做”，但政策制定者往往只停留在批评，没有建立规则。若 Flock 当年主动与“Have I Been Flocked”这类查询网站合作、修复漏洞并开放审计日志，局面会好得多。他还谈到伦理困境：在 Flock Forward 大会被拒后，他通过反编译 App 获取了完整嘉宾名单，但最终没有发布，而是报告给公司，以维持“不泄露 breach 数据”的原则。他认为长期坚持细微差别和伦理，虽然增长慢，却能建立信任。

访谈最后延伸到更广泛的隐私问题。Benn 提到数据经纪商 LexisNexis 掌握并被交易的海量个人数据，认为公众若了解其规模，对 Flock 的愤怒可能相形见绌。关于手机“偷听”阴谋论，他认为现实更可怕：平台未必在听你说话，而是通过行为数据、位置和交易记录预测你即将想什么；但到 2026 年，由于设备、智能手表和 AI 转录能力普及，已不能轻易排除监听。法律上“公共空间无隐私”的旧原则正被大规模聚合技术击穿。Flock 的问题可归纳为两个层面：一是私营数据库可被无控制地查询，必须立法监管；二是创业公司把不成熟技术“YOLO”式推向世界，缺乏安全最佳实践。即便 Axon 或 Motorola 安全性更好，第一层问题依然存在。Benn 的最终目标是推动“解决方案主义”：在民主社会中找到让所有人都不完全满意、但都能接受的折中路径，让公众回到地方政治、透明审计和可验证规则中，而不是把一家公司当作唯一敌人。

items.title: Google launches its ‘universal’ online shopping cart ahead of the holidays
items.description:
Save all of the products you’re browsing in one place. | Image: Google	

Google's intelligent AI shopping cart is finally here, and just in time to tempt users into Black Friday and seasonal holiday spending. Read the full story at The Verge.
items.content: Google’s intelligent AI shopping cart is finally here, and just in time to tempt users into Black Friday and seasonal holiday spending. The Universal Cart tool Google previewed at its I/O event in May is now rolling out in the US across the Gemini app and Google Search, with the aim of making it easier to stay organized and save money when shopping online.As the name suggests, it’s a “universal” digital cart that lets you save products from multiple retailers in a single unified space, and works across different Google platforms. That means you can find and add a bunch of products using the Gemini app and Google Search AI Mode, and they’ll all be saved to the same cart. There are also plans to integrate Universal Cart with Gmail and YouTube, but Google hasn’t announced a timeline for that yet.Here’s a demo of the checkout options for Universal Cart, which suggest you can’t check out multiple retailers simultaneously. GIF: GoogleGoogle will send you notifications about price drops and restocks for items saved in your cart, which spares you from having to check each retailer’s website individually, and can display any relevant promotional codes it finds besides the products you’ve saved. You can choose to pay for items from the cart using Google Wallet, or transfer them to the merchant’s own cart so you can checkout with the retailer directly. Together with Google Wallet, Universal Cart can also analyze the perks provided by each of your saved credit cards and help you choose the best payment method when purchasing.The launch comes as competition in the AI-assisted shopping space is heating up, with Google rivals including OpenAI and Meta having launched agentic AI assistants that can shop online on the user’s behalf. Shopify also recently announced that it’s opening its platform up to allow more AI agents to browse and purchase from Shopify listings. Big Tech players are entering this race on the bet that the future of online shopping involves having a robot do most of the work for you.
items.author: Jess Weatherbed
items.titleZh: 谷歌在假期前推出“通用”在线购物车
items.descriptionZh:
Google 在 5 月 I/O 活动上预览的智能 AI 购物车工具 Universal Cart 现已正式登陆美国市场，覆盖 Gemini 应用和 Google Search，时间点正好赶上黑色星期五与年末假日购物季。Google 希望借此让用户在网上购物时更容易保持条理并节省开支。

Universal Cart 的核心定位是一个“通用”数字购物车。用户可以从不同零售商那里保存商品，并统一放在同一个购物车空间中，同时该购物车可跨多个 Google 平台使用。也就是说，用户可以在 Gemini 应用和 Google Search 的 AI Mode 中寻找并添加商品，这些商品都会进入同一个购物车。Google 还计划未来把 Universal Cart 与 Gmail 和 YouTube 整合，但目前尚未公布具体时间表。

从功能上看，Universal Cart 有几项关键能力。第一，Google 会针对购物车中保存的商品发送降价和补货通知，用户不必再逐个访问零售商网站查看价格变化。第二，购物车会显示与已保存商品相关的促销代码，帮助用户获得额外折扣。第三，支付环节支持两种方式：用户可以用 Google Wallet 直接为购物车中的商品付款，也可以把商品转移到商家自己的购物车中，再通过零售商完成结账。结合 Google Wallet，Universal Cart 还能分析用户已保存信用卡所提供的权益，帮助选择更合适的支付方式。

不过，从演示中的结账选项来看，Universal Cart 目前似乎还不能让用户同时从多个零售商处一次性结账。它更像是一个跨平台、跨零售商的商品管理和支付辅助中心，而不是完全统一的“一键多商家结算”工具。原文也未披露支持零售商数量、用户规模、降价通知准确率、结账成功率或转化率等具体性能参数，因此暂时无法进行量化性能对比，只能从功能层面比较。

这项产品的推出背景是 AI 辅助购物竞争正在升温。Google 的竞争对手 OpenAI 和 Meta 都已经推出能够代表用户在线购物的代理式 AI 助手。Shopify 最近也宣布开放平台，允许更多 AI 代理浏览和购买其商品。大型科技公司正押注一个趋势：未来网上购物中，大部分繁琐工作将由机器人或 AI 代理完成。

Universal Cart 的创新点在于把 Google 的搜索、Gemini AI、AI Mode、Google Wallet 和通知系统整合进一个统一购物车体验中。它不只是保存链接，而是尝试覆盖“发现商品—添加商品—监控价格—显示优惠—选择支付—结账”的完整链路。应用场景包括假日购物、跨零售商比价、降价补货追踪、优惠码发现以及信用卡权益优化。更长期看，如果 Gmail 和 YouTube 整合落地，用户还可能从邮件收据、促销信息或视频内容中直接发现并添加商品。

总体而言，Universal Cart 是 Google 对 agentic commerce 趋势的回应。它利用 Google 生态的跨平台优势，试图在 AI 购物助手竞争中占据入口位置。但它的实际效果仍取决于零售商接入范围、跨商家结账体验、通知准确性以及用户对 Google 管理购物和支付数据的信任程度。

items.title: Malicious Russian disinformation bot traffic barely flinches after Ukraine strikes Yandex data centers and auto-migration kicks in
items.description: Ukraine's strikes on Russian data centers have caused legitimate bot traffic to go down, but malicious bots remain operational.
items.content: Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Reddit Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article 1 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter Russian bot traffic showed signs of slowing down after Ukraine bombed some of Yandex’s biggest data centers. Unfortunately, while the attacks have slowed down overall bot traffic from Russia, Cloudflare reports that malicious bots appeared to have simply transferred to other hosting ASNs like Radist and Selectel. Overall traffic on Yandex Search and Yandex.Cloud continues to stay at 10% to 15% of normal traffic levels, meaning the network remains disrupted. Cloudflare noted that traffic from the former is composed mostly of verified search crawlers indexing websites, meaning traffic from this service is mostly legitimate. On the other hand, the latter experienced a drop in malicious activities such as vulnerability scanning and probing after the data center bombings, but Cloudflare says that “high-volume automation did not vanish — it simply migrated to other hosting providers.”This was evident with one Cloudflare customer in the gambling sector: it saw malicious bot requests from Yandex.Cloud drop to zero but started seeing the same activity being routed through other networks. “Overall, Russian bot traffic targeting gambling accounts remained essentially flat over the week, moving from 167.7 million to 170.1 million requests (+1.4%),” the company wrote in its analysis. “The automation never stopped running; the operators simply migrated their workloads to alternate cloud providers once Yandex.Cloud became unavailable.”The company also looked at social media traffic and found a similar result — traffic from Russian-origin IPs only dropped by 0.6% in the same period while Russian bot traffic hitting “post,” “reply,” and “like” on one platform only decreased by 5.7%. Because of this, Cloudflare debunked the theory that Ukrainian strikes have caused a drop in social media manipulation, although it also noted that the scope of its analysis is limited to traffic that passed through Cloudflare services.Latest Videos FromTom's HardwareWatch full video here: Since cloud-based workloads can easily be transferred between data centers, taking a few out will not necessarily end the services running out of them. Instead, owners and operators could simply migrate to another data center, which is exactly what Amazon advised its clients who have been affected by Iranian strikes on AWS Bahrain and AWS Abu Dhabi.Cloudflare pointed out that this is why it’s difficult to defend against automated threats like bot networks — even though an IP prefix gets blocked or the physical infrastructure behind them gets annihilated, their operators could simply move their operations to another provider in a matter of hours and quickly return to normal traffic levels.
